Part 1 of 3 -- slides 151-158, 2 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slide set for Topic 11 (slides 151‑158) contains a concise definition of a Docker registry and explains its role in pulling and pushing images, including the default public Docker Hub and the option to run a private registry. This directly answers the question “What is a Docker registry?”.

The slides also list the Linux namespaces used by Docker, including the NET and USR namespaces. The NET namespace is described as providing each container with its own IP address and port space, while the USR namespace is described as mapping user names and UIDs, isolating user identity inside the container. This information is sufficient to answer the question about the difference between these two namespaces.

No additional context outside the topic’s slide range is required to answer either question, and the deck does not omit any relevant detail. Therefore, the deck adequately covers both questions.

Part 2 of 3 -- slides 161-172, 5 question(s): covered (confidence 0.35)

I examined the slide range 161‑172 for Topic 11 and the five matched student questions. The slides contain a clear illustration of namespace operations (slide 162) and explicit command examples for creating a veth pair, moving each end into a namespace, and assigning IPs (slides 172 and 173). The example in slide 173 also shows a concrete setup between two containers. While I did not read every slide in the surrounding range (e.g., slide 171) due to the step limit, the material I did review directly addresses each question. I also performed a few targeted searches (e.g., "veth pair namespace example", "container veth") that returned the same slides, confirming the coverage. Because the investigation was cut short before a full read‑through of all neighboring slides, I set a low confidence (0.35) but conclude the topic’s slides adequately cover the questions.

Part 3 of 3 -- slides 173-176, 4 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The four student questions matched to Topic 11 are all addressed within the slide range 173‑176. The slides provide a concise description of how chroot works—mounting a new directory and changing the process root—along with a brief explanation of the security limitation that allows a privileged process to escape a chroot. This directly answers the question "How does chroot work?". The difference between chroot and pivot_root is also covered: chroot simply changes the perceived root directory, whereas pivot_root detaches the new root and attaches it to the process root directory; the slides note that pivot_root is preferred because chroot can be escaped with the right capabilities, answering "Why is pivot_root often used instead of chroot?" and "What's the difference between chroot and pivot_root?". Finally, the slides include a definition of cgroups and their purpose—resource limiting and accounting for groups of processes—satisfying the question about what a cgroup is and its use. No additional search was required, as the content is fully present in the topic's own slides. Therefore, the topic provides complete coverage of the matched questions.
